questions.question: How would you build a responsive card layout without device-specific breakpoints?
questions.title: Responsive card layout without device breakpoints
questions.direct_answer: Use CSS Grid with repeat(auto-fit, minmax()) so the container creates as many usable card tracks as fit and wraps the rest. Give the minimum a container-safe value, use gap for spacing, and keep media flexible. This lets card count respond to available space without naming phone, tablet, or desktop widths.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner can translate a content constraint into a fluid Grid.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Copying device breakpoints or using a track minimum that overflows a narrow host.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Distinguish fluid track count from qualitative changes that still deserve a query.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Let each card's usable minimum determine when columns wrap.
auto-fit collapses empty tracks and stretches occupied tracks.
Use min(100%, minimum) to protect very narrow containers.
A media query is still valid when content relationships must change.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
I would begin with a Grid container and let its available inline size determine the column count. repeat(auto-fit, minmax()) creates as many repeated tracks as fit and moves remaining cards to the next row.

The minimum represents the narrowest useful card, not a device category. minmax(min(100%, 15rem), 1fr) keeps a card from becoming narrower than 15rem when room exists, while the inner min lets it fit if the entire container is narrower.

auto-fit collapses unused tracks, so a row with only two cards allows those cards to share the width. gap creates consistent parent-owned spacing, and max-width: 100% on images prevents media from establishing a wider box.

For example, the same component can show four columns in a wide page region, two inside a medium panel, and one inside a sidebar without reading the viewport width. A container query can add a qualitative card change if its internal relationship also needs to switch.

The boundary is layout meaning. This technique handles fluid column count, but it should not replace every media query. If navigation behaviour, reading order, or control labels need a distinct state, I add a condition for that actual content transition. I also test the final row with one item, because its stretching behaviour may not match the design. If cards should keep a capped width, an additional max-width or a different empty-track policy can preserve that intent.

sections.title: Turn card minimum width into the wrapping rule
sections.content: Instead of guessing a screen breakpoint, define the amount of space a card needs to remain useful. Grid creates another column only when that minimum, its gaps, and existing tracks fit inside the current container.

sections.title: Protect both wide and extremely narrow hosts
sections.content: A fixed minimum such as 15rem can overflow when the component is embedded in a container narrower than 15rem. Wrapping the minimum with min(100%, 15rem) caps it at the available track space. Test with one card as well as many cards because auto-fit and auto-fill differ most when tracks are empty.

sections.title: Track-count decision
sections.content:
Available container width
  -> fit another card minimum plus gap?
       yes -> create another column
       no  -> wrap next card
  -> distribute leftover width with 1fr

questions.question: How would you make a navigation menu usable with a keyboard and on small screens?
questions.title: Accessible responsive navigation menu
questions.direct_answer: Keep navigation destinations as links and use a real button to disclose the menu on small screens. The button must expose an accessible name, aria-expanded state, and aria-controls relationship; JavaScript synchronizes those with visibility. Preserve logical DOM order, visible focus, Escape handling where appropriate, and a usable no-script or wide-layout baseline.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner can combine native navigation semantics, disclosure state, and responsive presentation.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Calling a clickable div a menu button or letting aria-expanded drift from visual state.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Distinguish a disclosure from an application menubar and test scripting failure.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Navigation destinations remain anchor elements.
A real button controls menu disclosure.
aria-expanded must match the current visible state.
Keyboard focus order follows the DOM, not CSS visual order.
Visible focus and an Escape path support recovery.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
I keep the semantic jobs separate: nav identifies the region, anchors navigate to destinations, and a button controls whether the links are disclosed at constrained widths. A clickable div is not an equivalent menu button because it lacks native keyboard and button behaviour.

The button has a clear accessible name, aria-controls pointing to the links container, and aria-expanded matching the open state. JavaScript changes both visibility and aria-expanded together; CSS then presents the chosen state.

For example, activating the Menu button with Enter, Space, or a pointer reveals the links. Focus remains predictable, and pressing Escape can close the panel and return focus to the button when the navigation behaves as an overlay.

At wider widths, the links may remain visible and the disclosure button may be removed from presentation. The DOM order stays logical because CSS reordering would not update keyboard navigation order.

The boundary is widget complexity. A typical site navigation is a disclosure containing ordinary links, not an application menubar with arrow-key rules. I test keyboard-only operation, zoom, long translated labels, focus visibility, screen-reader state announcements, and behaviour when scripting fails. If the navigation opens as a modal drawer, that is a different interaction with stronger focus-management and dismissal requirements. I choose that pattern deliberately rather than turning every small-screen link list into a simulated dialog.

sections.title: Navigation plus disclosure, not a custom menubar
sections.content: The navigation region and its links work with native semantics. At a constrained size, a button adds one state: collapsed or expanded. Keeping that state explicit is simpler and more robust than inventing desktop-menu keyboard behaviour.

sections.title: State must agree across DOM, accessibility tree, and CSS
sections.content: A menu is broken when it is visually hidden but still focusable, visibly open while aria-expanded says false, or closed while focus remains trapped inside. Use one source of state to update the hidden attribute, expanded state, and focus behaviour. Avoid animating display itself; animate a suitable wrapper only after the semantic state is sound.

sections.title: Disclosure states
sections.content:
Collapsed: button aria-expanded=false | links hidden
Activate:  reveal links | set aria-expanded=true
Escape:    hide links | set aria-expanded=false | focus button
Wide mode: links visible in logical DOM order

questions.question: Why does a form submit when a secondary button is clicked?
questions.title: Unexpected form submission from a button
questions.direct_answer: A button element inside or associated with a form defaults to type=submit when type is omitted. A secondary control such as Preview, Add row, or Cancel therefore starts validation and submission unless it declares type=button. Fix the button's semantic type rather than relying on preventDefault everywhere.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner knows the missing-value default for a button associated with a form.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Adding preventDefault without correcting the button type.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Inspect form association and use the submitter when multiple real submit actions exist.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: button defaults to submit when it belongs to a form.
Secondary scripted actions should declare type=button.
The primary form action should explicitly declare type=submit.
preventDefault can mask the wrong semantic type.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
The first thing I inspect is the button type. A button element associated with a form uses submit as its missing-value default, so a visually secondary button can run constraint validation and trigger the form's submit event.

For example, an Add address button placed inside a checkout form may cause a network request when its type is omitted. Declaring type=button gives it no built-in form action, allowing its click handler to add the address fields only.

The intended primary action should declare type=submit explicitly. That makes both contracts visible in the markup and prevents a later refactor from changing behaviour simply because a component moved into a form.

I also inspect whether the button uses a form attribute that associates it with another form and whether a handler calls requestSubmit. Those mechanisms can cause legitimate submission even when DOM nesting is not obvious.

Calling preventDefault in every click handler is not the clean fix because keyboard activation or future code can still expose confusing semantics. The boundary is an intentional submitter: multiple submit buttons can be valid when their names, values, or formaction attributes represent distinct submission choices.

sections.title: Default semantics explain the surprise
sections.content: The browser is not treating every click as a submit. It is following the button element's default type inside a form. One explicit attribute corrects the control's native contract and removes the need for defensive event cancellation.

sections.title: Form submitter behavior
sections.content: The submit event's submitter property can identify the control that initiated submission. That is useful when a form legitimately has Save draft and Publish buttons. For a non-submission action, type=button remains the correct semantic fix and keeps the submit path reserved for actual form completion.

sections.title: Unexpected submission trace
sections.content:
Click secondary button
  -> type missing?
  -> button belongs to form
  -> missing type resolves to submit
  -> constraint validation
  -> submit event / request

sections.title: Give every form button an explicit job
sections.content:
```html
<form>
  <label for="item">Item</label>
  <input id="item" name="item" required>
  <button type="button" id="add-note">Add a note</button>
  <button type="submit" name="intent" value="save">Save order</button>
</form>
```
Add a note cannot submit by default; Save order is an explicit submitter and contributes intent=save.

questions.question: How do you prevent layout shift when responsive images load?
questions.title: Preventing image layout shift
questions.direct_answer: Provide correct width and height attributes on img so the browser can calculate an aspect ratio and reserve space before the file loads. Keep the image flexible with max-width: 100% and height: auto, or use aspect-ratio when dimensions come from another source. Reserved geometry prevents later content from being pushed down.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner connects intrinsic image dimensions to stable responsive layout.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Removing width and height because the CSS size is flexible or assuming lazy loading reserves space.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the separation between intrinsic ratio, responsive used size, and art-directed crops.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: img width and height establish an intrinsic aspect ratio.
CSS can still resize the image responsively.
height: auto preserves the source ratio with a flexible width.
Use aspect-ratio or a stable wrapper for dynamically sized media.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Layout shift occurs when the browser initially has no height for an image and discovers its dimensions only after downloading metadata. Content below is laid out too high, then moves when the image box gains height.

I include the source image's width and height attributes. Modern browsers use their ratio to reserve the appropriate space, while CSS can still make the image responsive with max-width: 100% and height: auto.

For example, an image file that is 1200 by 800 can keep those intrinsic attributes even when CSS displays it at 600 by 400 or at the full width of a smaller card. The ratio, not the literal rendered pixel size, is what reserves the box.

If the media ratio is known through data rather than the file attributes, aspect-ratio on a wrapper can reserve space. object-fit can control how a crop fills that box, but an intentional crop must not remove information required by the alt text.

The boundary is art direction. picture sources may have different crops and aspect ratios, so their dimensions must be tested carefully. Lazy loading reduces initial work but does not replace space reservation; an off-screen image can still shift content when approached.

sections.title: Reserve geometry before bytes arrive
sections.content: The browser can lay out a stable page when it knows the image ratio in advance. Responsive sizing changes the final width, and the ratio supplies the corresponding height before the selected resource finishes loading.

sections.title: Intrinsic dimensions are metadata, not a fixed CSS size
sections.content: HTML width and height attributes contribute an intrinsic ratio, while the CSS sizing algorithm determines the used size. max-width: 100% prevents oversizing and height: auto derives height from that ratio. This combination keeps both responsiveness and stability.

sections.title: Layout with reserved image space
sections.content:
Parse img dimensions -> reserve ratio box -> lay out following text
Select responsive candidate -> download -> paint inside reserved box
Result: following text keeps the same position

sections.title: Keep a responsive image's aspect ratio reserved
sections.content: ```html ``` The rendered image can shrink, but its 3:2 ratio is available before the chosen file loads.

questions.question: How do you find and fix unexpected horizontal scrolling on a mobile page?
questions.title: Debugging mobile horizontal scrolling
questions.direct_answer: Reproduce the narrow width, locate the first element whose bounding box crosses the viewport, and inspect its computed size and positioning. Typical causes are width: 100% plus content-box padding, fixed or min-content widths, 100vw, unwrapped text, media, Grid or Flex minimums, and transforms. Fix that element locally instead of hiding overflow on the whole page.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the learner can turn a responsive bug into a measured, local diagnosis.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Adding overflow-x: hidden to body and declaring the layout fixed.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Check focus reachability and classify geometry, intrinsic, layout, and positioning causes separately.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Identify the exact element crossing the viewport.
Separate box-size, intrinsic-content, track, and positioning causes.
Check min-width: auto in Flexbox and Grid children.
Do not use global overflow-x: hidden as the diagnosis.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
I reproduce the smallest width that shows the scrollbar, then find which element crosses the viewport. A temporary outline on page descendants or comparing each element's bounding rectangle with documentElement.clientWidth can reveal the first offender.

I inspect box arithmetic next. width: 100% under content-box grows beyond its parent when horizontal padding or border is added. A width of 100vw can also include space differently from the document's visible content area and is often unnecessary for an ordinary full-width block.

Then I inspect intrinsic content and layout minimums. A large image, table, pre element, long URL, fixed Grid track, or Flex/Grid child's automatic min-width can keep a box wider than the screen. For example, min-width: 0 plus a suitable wrapping rule can release a text column without clipping it.

Positioning is another category: absolute offsets, transforms, negative margins, or decorative pseudo-elements may paint beyond the right edge. I test focus as well, because an off-screen focused control is more serious than a decorative pixel.

I fix the owning component with border-box, a flexible max width, minmax(0, 1fr), min-width: 0, wrapping, or a contained data scroller. overflow-x: hidden on body is a last resort because it can hide evidence, clip focus indicators, and leave unreachable content. After the local fix, I repeat the test with long localized text and 200 percent zoom. Both can recreate the same intrinsic-width pressure even when the original English fixture now fits.

sections.title: Measure the offender, then classify the cause
sections.content: Horizontal scrolling is caused by at least one box extending beyond the scroll container. Locating that box turns a vague mobile problem into one of four concrete categories: declared geometry, intrinsic content, layout minimums, or visual positioning.

sections.title: Automate the first pass, inspect the result
sections.content: A console loop can report elements whose left or right bounding edge lies outside the viewport, but nested descendants may all be reported because one ancestor is misplaced. Start with the outermost meaningful offender and inspect computed width, min-width, transforms, and its containing block before changing CSS.

sections.title: Horizontal-scroll investigation
sections.content:
Reproduce narrow width
  -> find box beyond viewport
  -> width + padding? -> border-box / correct width
  -> intrinsic minimum? -> min-width: 0 + content rule
  -> fixed media/track? -> flexible constraint
  -> transform/offset? -> correct positioning
  -> retest focus, zoom, and nearby widths
